Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

could you turn these notes into a clear prompt for comparing the two possible routes for our spring outings? we're the Riverside Blocks Birding Circle, a volunteer-run urban birding group. usually 18 to 24 people come, from first-time birders to people who have kept lists for years. we're looking at a six-week run of Sunday morning walks, and the usual outing is about two hours. compare the Canal Loop and the Foundry Greenway using the criteria in these notes, not just which one sounds prettier. we'd like a useful comparison for the route-planning meeting, not a finished calendar or a field guide. Keep the difference between what we know and what we're guessing, because a few of these details still need checking.

Some background on the group: we meet near the central library, but people arrive from several neighborhoods and not everyone drives. We have binoculars to lend, though only eight pairs, and two volunteer leaders have offered to lead the series. One leader is comfortable identifying common birds by call; the other prefers visual identification and likes to stop for beginners' questions. We don't have a formal rule that the whole group has to stay together, but on busy paths we normally try. Our last spring series had 21 people on its first walk and 16 on the last one. That's context for thinking about crowding, not a prediction that the same number will come this time.

1) Canal Loop notes: the route is listed as 2.1 miles if we use the footbridge and return along the north bank. The map we have is from last autumn, and it marks the towpath as mostly level, with a short ramp near the old pump house. There are three benches shown, but one volunteer says the bench nearest the water was removed; we haven't confirmed that. The meeting point is about a seven-minute walk from Harbor Street bus stop. The stop is served by two routes on Sundays, according to the timetable someone checked in February. I don't know whether the service has changed since then. There is a public restroom in the marina building, but the marina page only says its hours vary by season. Please don't say it's open for our walks as if that were confirmed.

The Canal Loop has water, a narrow strip of trees, and planted beds beside the path. Last April, two members noted swallows over the water and several warblers in the trees. Those are sightings from one visit, not a promise about what we'll see this spring. The towpath can be noisy when delivery trucks use the nearby service road, especially around 9 a.m., but we don't have a noise log. A member who walks there often said, “the water makes the route feel open, but the path gets pinched by the railings near the lock.” That quote is one person's impression, and the narrow section might matter if the group is large. The map labels the footbridge as accessible, though no one in our group has checked the surface or approach recently.

2) Foundry Greenway notes: our draft route is 1.6 miles, using the paved loop through the former rail yard and the small wetland pocket, with an optional short spur to the community garden. The spur would add about a quarter mile, but the garden gate is sometimes locked; we have not asked the garden volunteers about Sunday access. A bus stop is at the east entrance, with one Sunday route listed in the transit app. The same app shows a longer walk from the central library than for the Canal Loop, but it doesn't account for where individual members start. There is a restroom in the recreation center across Foundry Avenue. A member says it was open on a recent Sunday, but we haven't confirmed hours for the spring dates.

The Foundry route has young trees, grasses, a drainage pond, and the garden if the spur is open. Two members saw red-winged blackbirds at the pond in March last year, and the garden coordinator told us there are often finches near the seed beds. The coordinator's comment wasn't a survey and doesn't guarantee birds will be there during our outings. The paved loop is described in the city brochure as smooth; one walker mentioned a sharp turn where the path meets the east entrance. There are picnic tables near the pond and a roofed shelter by the recreation center. The tables are usually occupied by lunchtime, according to one member. We don't know how busy the route is at 8:30 a.m. or whether any current construction affects it. Traffic from Foundry Avenue is audible near the entrance, but people who've walked farther into the loop say it gets quieter.

Please compare both options on distance and likely walking pace for a mixed-experience group, transit access based on the notes, surfaces and accessibility questions, habitat variety and the limits of the bird-sighting information, places to pause or shelter, restroom certainty, and possible noise or crowding. Include the group size and two-hour Sunday-morning context when it helps, without treating last year's attendance or sightings as guaranteed. The workshop is an independent neighborhood business with a small service area, a front counter, and a narrow back room where repairs are carried out. It has two mechanics, Mara and Luis, and a part-time counter worker, Nia. The shop handles everyday maintenance as well as more complicated repairs, but the available space and work stands are limited. On a rainy Tuesday morning, three customers arrive within about twenty minutes. One needs a flat tire fixed before commuting home, another has brought in a used bicycle with shifting problems, and a parent asks whether a child’s bike can be made safe before the weekend. The shop’s appointment book already has two jobs listed for the afternoon.

Mara is working on a touring bicycle whose owner reported that the rear brake felt inconsistent on a long ride. Luis has begun inspecting the used bicycle. Nia is answering the phone and checking in the walk-in customers. The parent says, “I don’t need anything fancy; I just want to know it’s safe.” Nia writes down the concern but is unsure how much inspection time to promise while both mechanics are occupied. A customer waiting by the counter asks whether a quick tire repair can be done immediately. Nia says she will check, rather than giving a definite time.

As Luis examines the used bicycle, he notices that the chain skips under pressure and that the rear derailleur hanger appears bent. He tells the customer that the shifting issue may involve more than a simple adjustment. The customer replies, “The seller said it only needed a tune-up.” Luis has not yet checked whether replacement parts are available, and he does not want to estimate the full cost before inspecting the drivetrain more closely. He explains that he can report what he finds before doing work beyond the initial inspection. The customer asks whether the bicycle will be ready that day, but no completion time has been promised.

Meanwhile, Mara finds wear on the touring bicycle’s brake pads and a loose cable housing. She can address those items, but the owner’s description of inconsistent braking makes her want to inspect the rest of the brake system before saying that the problem is resolved. The owner is due to collect the bicycle later that afternoon and asks, “Can you just tighten it so I can get back on the road?” Mara answers that she will check the brake carefully first and then explain what she can confirm. The conversation is brief, and the owner looks at the appointment book on the counter while she returns to the repair stand.

At the front counter, the flat-tire customer explains that they have to leave for work at a fixed time and asks whether the shop can fit the repair in. Nia knows that a puncture can sometimes be handled quickly, but she has not checked the wheel or confirmed whether the inner tube is repairable. She also knows that interrupting a repair can affect the jobs already underway. She asks the customer to wait while she checks with the mechanics. At that moment, the phone rings again, and a caller asks about the price of a tune-up. Nia takes the caller’s name and number rather than quoting a price without confirming what service is needed.

Use the episode to develop questions that invite discussion of communication, workload, uncertainty, customer expectations, and decisions about what to inspect or promise. Keep the questions open-ended and grounded in the details; avoid assuming that a customer is unreasonable, that a staff member made a mistake, or that a particular repair should take priority. Include questions about what information the staff may need before setting a time or price, how they might explain limits without dismissing a customer’s concern, and how the team could coordinate when several requests arrive at once. It is fine for some questions to ask participants what they would do, provided they distinguish their own preferences from facts stated in the episode.

Please organize the discussion questions under these numbered sections:
1. What each person knows, needs, and expects
2. Communication at the counter and in the repair area
3. Choices about inspection, timing, and workload
4. Possible next steps and information still needed

Include several questions in each section, with a mix of questions about specific moments and broader questions that connect those moments. Do not add a new customer, a new repair problem, an agreement, a completed repair, or any other event that is not described here. The discussion should remain useful even if participants disagree about what the shop should do first.
